title: Earl Hines band personnel: Walter Fuller and the "Rosetta" re-creation
summary: Day two begins with Walter Fuller, who sang "Rosetta," a late-1960s recreation of the record, and other Hines men like Quinn Wilson.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Yesterday we were talking about Earl Hines and some of the members of the band (inaudible). I think we started to talk about Walter Fuller.

Yes, we did. And Walter was a very fine trumpet player with Earl and he was a good singer. He sang, you know, he had a jazz style of singing. And he tried to pattern somewhat after Louis, Louis Armstrong. But he had a high voice, a much higher voice than Lou. And he sang things with Earl, some of his popular things. "Rosetta" was one thing I remember in particular. It was a very popular record that Earl had out. And Walter Fuller sang the chorus on this. And it was a wonderful chorus that he did. In fact, they did a recreation of that -- Earl's particular record and they sent for me to come to -- from Honolulu to Decca -- Capitol Records did -- to come back to Hollywood. This was -- oh, this was probably about '67 or '68 -- and recreate Fuller's vocal chorus. I had to learn it all over again.

And I told them to get Fuller since Fuller was right in San Diego, but evidently they couldn't get in touch with him. And that's the way record companies do business anyway. But they had some fine -- other fine musicians in there too. There was Wally Bishop, the drummer, and I mentioned him previously. But he wound up in Europe. He's in Europe now. In fact, he was living in Amsterdam the last I heard about him,
and he was doing quite a bit of playing with different groups over in Europe. And whenever an artist came to Europe and he didn't bring his own band, well, he would back him over in Europe.

Also in the same band was a fine guitar player. He's passed away since. Lawrence Dixon was his name. And we had another fine trumpet player who doubled on alto saxophone, George Dixon. He was another fine man in that band. And, of course, there were three of us trombone players and I mentioned previously that two of these guys have passed away now. And that would be Billy Franklin and Louis Taylor.

And, of course, let me see. There was a bass player in there, Quinn Wilson. He did -- he was a good arranger. We call him Cupie. And he did quite a bit of writing for Earl back in those days. And he played a string bass and he also played a tuba. And he was a wonderful soloist on tuba, and Earl featured him quite a bit.
